sections.title: Detailed Brief Overview
rows: What
The **Judicial Structure** of India comprising the apex **Supreme Court** and state-level **High Courts** forming an integrated judicial system.
When
**Supreme Court** inaugurated on **January 28, 1950**; First **High Court** (Calcutta) established in **1862**.
Where
**Supreme Court** located in **New Delhi**; **High Courts** established across various states/union territories.
Who
Headed by the **Chief Justice of India (CJI)** at the apex level and **Chief Justices** at individual High Courts.
Constitutional Basis
Part V (Articles **124-147**) for **Supreme Court**; Part VI (Articles **214-231**) for **High Courts**.
Why Important
Protector of **Fundamental Rights**, guardian of the **Constitution**, and final interpreter of laws.
Key Features
**Single integrated judicial system**, **Judicial Review**, **Writ Jurisdiction (Article 32 & 226)**, and **Public Interest Litigation (PIL)**.
Significance for UPSSSC PET
High-scoring static GK area covering article numbers, retirement ages, appointment processes, and landmark judgments.

items.title: Supreme Court Organization and Composition
items.content:
• Started in **1950** with **1 Chief Justice and 7 other judges** (Total 8).
• Current sanctioned strength is **34 judges** (**1 CJI + 33 other judges**).
• Appointed by the **President of India** under **Article 124(2)**.
• Retirement age for Supreme Court judges is **65 years**.
• **Mnemonic for SC Articles:** **'J'**ust **'S'**upreme **'C'**ourt (**J**urisdiction, **S**eats, **C**onstitution) -> Articles **124 to 147**.

items.title: High Court Organization and Composition
items.content:
• Established under **Article 214** (one High Court for each state, though Parliament can establish a common High Court for two or more states).
• Currently, there are **25 High Courts** in India.
• Appointed by the **President of India** in consultation with the **CJI** and the **Governor** of the state.
• Retirement age for High Court judges is **65 years** (increased from 60 by the **15th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1963**).
• **Mnemonic for HC Articles:** **'H'**igh **'C'**ourt **'A'**uthority (**H**C, **C**ommon, **A**ppointment) -> Articles **214 to 231**.

items.title: Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
items.content:
• **Original Jurisdiction (Article 131):** Federal disputes between Centre and States or between States.
• **Writ Jurisdiction (Article 32):** Enforcement of Fundamental Rights by issuing writs (Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo-Warranto).
• **Appellate Jurisdiction (Articles 132-136):** Constitutional, Civil, Criminal appeals and Special Leave Petition (SLP).
• **Advisory Jurisdiction (Article 143):** President can seek legal advice from the Supreme Court.
• **Court of Record (Article 129):** Power to punish for contempt of court.

items.title: Jurisdiction of the High Court
items.content:
• **Original Jurisdiction:** Disputes relating to maritime, divorce, contempt of court, and election petitions.
• **Writ Jurisdiction (Article 226):** Wider than Supreme Court as it covers both Fundamental Rights and **legal rights**.
• **Appellate Jurisdiction:** Civil and criminal appeals against subordinate court rulings.
• **Supervisory Jurisdiction (Article 227):** Power of superintendence over all subordinate courts and tribunals within its territorial jurisdiction.
• **Control over Subordinate Judiciary (Articles 233-237):** Appointment, posting, and promotion of district judges.

items.title: Judicial Review and PIL Concept
items.content:
• **Judicial Review:** Power of judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive orders (Derived from **Article 13**).
• **Public Interest Litigation (PIL):** Introduced in the early **1980s** by **Justice P.N. Bhagwati** and **Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer**.
• Relaxed the rule of **'Locus Standi'** (any public-spirited person can move the court on behalf of oppressed/marginalized classes).

Habeas Corpus
'To have the body of'
Writ used to secure the release of a person detained unlawfully.
Mandamus
'We Command'
Writ issued to a public official to perform a mandatory duty.
Certiorari
'To be certified'
Writ issued by a higher court to a lower court to quash an order.
Quo-Warranto
'By what authority'
Writ issued to prevent illegal usurpation of a public office.

items.definition: Remember the five writs using the acronym **H-M-P-C-Q**: **H**abeas Corpus, **M**andamus, **P**rohibition, **C**ertiorari, and **Q**uo-Warranto.

items.term: Trick 2: SC vs HC Article Numbers (124 vs 214)
items.definition: Supreme Court starts around Article **124** (add 90 to get High Court starting article **214**).

items.term: Trick 3: Retirement Ages (SC vs HC History)
items.definition: Both Supreme Court and High Court judges retire at **65 years** currently (Note: HC retirement age was raised from **60 to 65** by the **15th Amendment, 1963**).
Think of **BP** (Bharat Petroleum) for PIL pioneers: **B**hagwati and **P**.N. / **K**rishna Iyer.
Always remember that **both** Supreme Court and High Court judges are officially appointed by the **President of India**, NOT the Prime Minister or Chief Minister.
Supreme Court as Court of Record is under **Article 129**, while High Court as Court of Record is under **Article 215**.

items.term: Mistake 1: Confusing Article 32 and Article 226 Scope
items.definition: Students often think Article 32 has a wider scope than Article 226. Correct fact: **Article 226** has a wider scope because High Courts can issue writs for **Fundamental Rights AND legal rights**, whereas Supreme Court (Article 32) is restricted only to **Fundamental Rights**.

Students confuse Supreme Court's Original Jurisdiction with civil/criminal appeals. Correct fact: **Article 131** covers *only* federal disputes (Centre vs States or State vs State), not ordinary civil or criminal disputes.

items.term: Mistake 3: High Court Retirement Age Trap
items.definition: Many static books or older notes state High Court retirement age is **60 years**. Correct fact: It was amended to **65 years** in **1963** by the **15th Constitutional Amendment Act**.
Judges are **appointed** by the **President**, but they take their **oath** before the **President** (for SC) or the **Governor** (for HC).

items.term: Mistake 5: Origin of PIL in Constitution
items.definition: Students assume PIL is explicitly mentioned in the Constitution. Correct fact: PIL is a **judicial innovation** and is not mentioned anywhere in the original text of the Constitution.
India has a **single integrated judicial system** with the **Supreme Court** at the apex, followed by **High Courts**, and **Subordinate Courts** at the bottom.
Sanctioned strength is **34 judges** (**1 CJI + 33 judges**), revised by Parliament under the **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2019**.
Judges can be removed by the **President** only after an address passed by **each House of Parliament** supported by a **special majority** on grounds of proved misbehavior or incapacity.
There are **25 High Courts** in India, with **Guwahati High Court** having jurisdiction over multiple North-Eastern states.
The **Allahabad High Court** (located in UP) is the **largest High Court** in India in terms of sanctioned judge strength and territorial jurisdiction.
Appointed under **Article 127** by the CJI with the previous consent of the President when there is a lack of quorum of permanent judges in the Supreme Court.
Appointed under **Article 126** (for Supreme Court) and **Article 223** (for High Court) by the President when the office of Chief Justice is vacant.
Transferred by the **President** of India after consultation with the **Chief Justice of India** under **Article 222**.
Governed by Articles **233 to 237** under Part VI of the Constitution, ensuring independence of the lower judiciary from the executive.
Secured through **security of tenure**, **fixed service conditions**, **prohibition of discussion on conduct of judges in legislature**, and **power to punish for contempt**.

upscNotes.content: For UPSSSC PET, focus heavily on exact article numbers (Article 32, 124, 214, 226), retirement ages (65 years for both SC and HC), and total sanctioned strength (34 for SC, 25 High Courts).
Do not confuse the writ jurisdiction scope: Article 226 (High Court) is wider than Article 32 (Supreme Court) because High Courts protect legal rights alongside fundamental rights.
Remember that the Allahabad High Court is of prime importance for UP-specific competitive exams like UPSSSC PET. Know its location, bench details, and establishment year (1866).
Avoid marking '60 years' as the retirement age for High Court judges; it was increased to 65 years by the 15th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1963.

keyTakeaways: Supreme Court Articles: **124 to 147** (Part V); High Court Articles: **214 to 231** (Part VI).
Current Supreme Court judge strength is **34**; Total number of High Courts is **25**.
Retirement age is **65 years** for judges of both Supreme Court and High Courts.
Article 32 (Supreme Court) deals with Fundamental Rights writs; Article 226 (High Court) deals with both Fundamental Rights and legal rights writs.
PIL was introduced in the **1980s** relaxing the rule of **Locus Standi**, pioneered by Justices P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer.
Allahabad High Court is the largest High Court in India by judge strength.
